::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[other form of uv notation of integration by parts](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1293143/other-form-of-uv-notation-of-integration-by-parts), asked by [Kirbies](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/157598/kirbies) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2015-05-21; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> So integration by parts looks like this 
>
> $\int u\, dv = uv - \int v\, du$
>
> But I have often seen it like this:
>
> $\int uv\,dx = u \int v\, dx - \int (u'\int v dx )\, dx$
>
> I cannot prove this.  
>
> $uv = \int v\, dx$ is trivial
>
>
> $\int v\, du = \int (u'\int v dx )\, dx$  can be seen by substituting in $du = u'\,dx$ 
>
> But when it comes to showing $\int u\,dv = \int uv\,dx$ I get stuck.  How would I do this?
:::

I think you're getting tripped up because the $v$ used in each identity is different.  To see why, use each to evaluate $\int x \cos x\,dx$.  In the second identity, $v=\cos x$.  But in the first identity, $dv=\cos x\,dx$, so $v=\sin x$.

Rather, you can prove the second identity by showing that the derivative of the of right-hand side is $uv$.
Since $\left(\int v\,dx\right)' = v$, etc., we have
$$\left(u \int v\,dx - \int u' \int v \,dx\right)'
    = u' \int v\,dx + u v - u' \int v\,dx = uv$$
